concepts.name: Statutory Basis and Establishment of NHRC
key_dimensions: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 — parent legislation and its amendments (2006, 2019)
Distinction between constitutional body vs. statutory body — NHRC has no constitutional backing unlike Election Commission
Paris Principles (1991) compliance — how NHRC derives its 'A-status' accreditation from UN
Comparison with SHRC — both under same Act but different provisions govern each

concepts.name: Composition of NHRC: Chairperson Eligibility
key_dimensions: Pre-2019 amendment: only retired Chief Justice of India eligible as Chairperson
Post-2019 amendment: retired CJI OR any retired Judge of Supreme Court eligible — a key UPSC trap
Appointment authority: President of India on recommendation of a High-Powered Committee
Contrast with SHRC Chairperson: retired Chief Justice of a High Court — frequent comparison question

concepts.name: High-Powered Committee for NHRC Appointments
key_dimensions: Composition: Prime Minister (Chair), Speaker of Lok Sabha, Home Minister, Leaders of Opposition in both Houses
Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha is a member — often confused with Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice President)
Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha inclusion — ensures bipartisan oversight
Contrast with appointment committee for CBI Director or CEC — frequent overlap trap

concepts.name: Members of NHRC: Number, Eligibility, and 2019 Amendments
key_dimensions: Pre-2019: 4 members (2 retired SC judges + 2 from human rights backgrounds)
Post-2019 amendment: up to 5 members; at least one woman member mandatory — new addition
Ex-officio members: Chairpersons of National Commissions (NCW, NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCBC, NCPCR) — 2019 added NCBC and NCPCR
Distinction between full members and ex-officio members in voting/quorum contexts

concepts.name: Tenure and Service Conditions of NHRC Members
key_dimensions: Term: 3 years or until age 70, whichever is earlier — not 5 years (common misconception)
No re-appointment after completing term — ensures independence
Removal: only by Presidential order after Supreme Court inquiry (similar to removal of SC judge process)
Salary and conditions: charged to Consolidated Fund of India — signals financial autonomy

concepts.name: Jurisdiction of NHRC: Subject-Matter Scope
key_dimensions: Mandate covers violations of human rights or abetment thereof by State or its agents
Definition of 'human rights' under PHR Act: rights relating to life, liberty, equality, dignity guaranteed by Constitution or embodied in International Covenants
NHRC can act suo motu, on petition, or on reference from courts
Cannot investigate matters older than 1 year from the alleged violation — strict limitation (key trap)

concepts.name: Territorial and Institutional Jurisdiction Limitations
key_dimensions: NHRC cannot investigate complaints against armed forces — Section 19 of PHR Act is a critical exception
For armed forces: can only seek a report from Central Government and make recommendations; no direct inquiry
Complaints against State Governments can be taken up if SHRC is not constituted in that state
NHRC cannot investigate matters pending before SHRCs or other commissions — avoids jurisdictional overlap

concepts.name: NHRC vs. SHRC: Concurrent and Exclusive Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: NHRC can transfer a complaint to SHRC if it relates to a state subject — division of labor
SHRC cannot investigate complaints against Central Government employees — exclusive NHRC domain
If SHRC is not constituted in a state, NHRC assumes jurisdiction for that state — fill-in provision
Both bodies lack enforcement power — recommendations only, a shared structural weakness

concepts.name: Powers of NHRC During Inquiry
key_dimensions: Powers of a Civil Court under Code of Civil Procedure — can summon witnesses, receive evidence, requisition documents
Can visit any institution under State control (jails, detention centers) for inspection
Can utilize services of any officer or investigation agency of Central or State Government
Can call for information or report from Central/State Government within specified time — government is bound to respond

concepts.name: Remedial Powers and Recommendations of NHRC
key_dimensions: NHRC can recommend: payment of compensation, prosecution of officials, or amendment of laws/rules
Cannot impose compensation directly — only recommends; government must comply or explain (quasi-judicial, not judicial)
Can approach Supreme Court or High Court for directions if recommendations are not implemented
Distinction from court: NHRC orders are recommendatory, not binding — a frequent UPSC conceptual trap

concepts.name: Interim Relief Powers of NHRC
key_dimensions: Can grant interim relief to complainant during pendency of inquiry
Can approach SC/HC for stay orders or directions on behalf of victim
Contrast with National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission — NCDRC has more binding interim powers
Interim relief power distinguishes NHRC from purely advisory bodies like NCPRI

concepts.name: Annual Report and Accountability Mechanism
key_dimensions: NHRC submits annual report to Central Government and concerned State Governments
Reports are laid before Parliament/State Legislature along with a memorandum of action taken
No provision for Parliament to debate or vote on NHRC recommendations — limits democratic accountability
Contrast with CAG reports: CAG reports are examined by PAC; NHRC reports have no equivalent scrutiny committee

concepts.name: NHRC and International Human Rights Instruments
key_dimensions: PHR Act incorporates rights from ICCPR and ICESCR into domestic law through definitional inclusion
NHRC represents India at international human rights forums — diplomatic function beyond domestic inquiry
Paris Principles compliance: independence, broad mandate, adequate resources, accessible to public
NHRC's 'A-status' under Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) — implication for UN engagement

concepts.name: Complaints Procedure and Admissibility Conditions
key_dimensions: Complaint must be filed within 1 year of the alleged violation — cannot condone delay beyond this (unlike courts)
Complaints can be filed in any language recognized under 8th Schedule — accessibility provision
Anonymous complaints: NHRC may or may not act — discretionary unlike RTI where anonymous complaints are rejected outright
NHRC cannot investigate matters where complainant has an alternative remedy pending — judicial restraint principle

concepts.name: Role of NHRC in Custodial Deaths and Encounter Killings
key_dimensions: State governments must mandatorily report custodial deaths and rape within 24 hours to NHRC
Non-reporting itself constitutes a violation — NHRC can take suo motu cognizance
NHRC guidelines on encounter killings: mandatory magisterial inquiry, report to NHRC — 1997 guidelines
Tension with Section 19 (armed forces exemption): paramilitary forces in civilian areas create grey zone

concepts.name: NHRC and Prison Reforms: Inspection Powers
key_dimensions: NHRC or its representatives can visit any jail or institution where persons are detained to study living conditions
Prior notice to State Government required — unlike some emergency inspection powers
Recommendations on prison conditions are non-binding but politically significant
Contrast with Supreme Court's inherent power to inspect — SC can act without prior notice and issue binding directions

concepts.name: Structural Criticisms and Independence Concerns
key_dimensions: NHRC depends on government for staff and investigation agencies — structural dependence undermines independence
Chairperson and members appointed by a committee dominated by ruling party — potential executive influence
Cannot investigate armed forces — largest source of rights complaints in conflict zones remains outside purview
Recommendations are non-binding — described as 'toothless tiger' in academic and civil society discourse

concepts.name: Distinction Between NHRC and Human Rights Courts
key_dimensions: PHR Act mandates establishment of Human Rights Courts at district level — separate from NHRC
Human Rights Courts: designated Sessions Courts, with Special Public Prosecutor appointed by State Government
NHRC vs. Human Rights Courts: NHRC is quasi-judicial/recommendatory; Human Rights Courts have criminal trial powers
Human Rights Courts are grossly underutilized — most states have not operationalized them (governance failure angle)

concepts.name: 2019 Amendment Act: Key Changes and UPSC Implications
key_dimensions: Chairperson eligibility expanded from 'retired CJI only' to 'retired CJI or retired SC judge' — most tested change
Mandatory woman member introduced — affirmative representation in composition
Ex-officio members expanded: NCBC Chairperson and NCPCR Chairperson added to existing list
Term of office for Chairperson/members remains unchanged at 3 years/70 years — common misconception that 2019 changed tenure

concepts.name: NHRC's Role During Disasters and Mass Atrocities
key_dimensions: NHRC has taken suo motu cognizance in post-Godhra riots (2002), Manipur encounters, and COVID-19 migrant crisis
Can seek reports from state governments on preventive action and relief measures
Limitation: cannot punish state officials directly — political accountability gap
Comparison with National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA): NDMA has statutory powers to direct; NHRC only recommends — different enforcement architecture
